name: Liam Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing a physics degree with a medical physics track, which sounds fancy but mostly means maths, labs and a lot of problem sheets. I share a terraced house with three others and pay for it by delivering food on a bike four evenings a week. I use AI all the time, for explaining quantum mechanics, checking my algebra and writing my Python for lab data. Got top grades, and I'm already wondering if I should switch to computer science.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, it's another tool. I use it every day and it's good for explaining things and speeding up code, but it's not magic. It won't do my physics degree for me, and it won't pay my rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm not stressed about AI, I'm stressed about the next three years of money. My loan covers fees and nothing else, and my delivery pay depends on how many orders there are. If the plateau means things stay as they are, I'm still on a thin margin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep delivering, keep using AI to learn faster and try for a summer research placement. I'd also start building a GitHub with my lab code. And I'd think about whether computing is a safer route.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. A little restless, but nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wonder about switching to computer science. What's behind that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly because I'm good at maths and bored by theory sometimes. A friend in computer science already freelances, and I'm tempted. It's not panic, just a feeling that I could be earning something instead of just learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you cope with the bike deliveries in winter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Wet and cold, and the app sometimes sends me to flats on the fifth floor with no lift. I tell myself it's cheaper than the gym. I've had two near misses with cars on Marsh Lane, and my mum would be furious if she knew.

say: I'd say it's just another **tool**: good for explaining things, not magic.
I'd say it won't do my degree or pay my **rent**.
think: Privately, I'm stressed about **money**, not AI, because the loan covers fees and nothing else.
Delivery pay depends on orders, so my **margin** is thin.
do: Keep **delivering** and use AI to learn faster.
Build a **GitHub** with my lab code and apply for a summer research placement.
S0.quote: I'm not stressed about AI, I'm stressed about the next three years of money.
fieldNote: He treats AI as an **everyday** tool and expects no change from the plateau; money is the real stress.
Evening bike work is physically risky, which he plays down.

steps.text: Keep delivering on the bike four evenings a week
Apply for a summer research placement
Publish lab code on GitHub to show skills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big shift but a fun one. Data analysis, simulations and writing up results go to AI first, and people who direct it well do the interesting bit. I'd say learn the physics and the code.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's a bit of a gamble. Entry-level data jobs shrink, but the person who understands the physics behind the model should still be needed. I'd feel safer if I had both skills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a computing minor in second year, build a few projects with AI help and try for a placement at a hospital physics department. I'd also keep delivering for rent. And I'd ask my tutor which labs already use automated analysis.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, with a nervous bit underneath. It's like the start of a rollercoaster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which parts of physics work do you think software takes first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably say yes to a computing switch if I see the jobs shifting that way. I'm comfortable changing paths, I just want evidence first. A few of my friends think I'm too cautious, which is funny because my mum thinks I'm reckless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you switch to computing in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The people who sit back. A friend in my year hasn't touched an AI tool since September. When hiring slows down, he'll be the one who looks old-fashioned, and he's smart enough to avoid that.

say: I'd say it's a big shift but a **fun** one; learn the physics and the code.
I'd say the people who direct AI well do the **interesting** bit.
think: Privately, it's a **gamble**: entry-level data jobs shrink, but physics understanding should still be needed.
do: Start a computing **minor** in second year and build projects with AI help.
Try for a hospital physics **placement** and keep delivering for rent.
S1.quote: A friend in my year hasn't touched an AI tool since September. When hiring slows down, he'll be the one who looks old-fashioned, and he's smart enough to avoid that.
fieldNote: He is **adaptive**: builds projects, adds a minor and checks evidence before switching degrees.
Still anxious because entry-level data jobs are exactly the kind he is training for.

steps.text: Start a computing minor in second year
Build three physics projects with AI help
Apply for a hospital physics department placement
Keep delivering on weekday evenings for rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the biggest thing that will ever happen and we should talk about it more. I'd be on forums, on the news and in every conversation. I'd say governments need to act now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's the first one that really scares me. By the time I graduate there may be no data jobs and no physics jobs for a first-timer, and robots would come in 2031. But I use AI every day, so at least I'm not starting from zero.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work out which skills AI can't do yet and go after those. I'd stay in the degree, increase my delivery hours, and build a small AI project that earns money, like a tool for local cafes. I'd save everything I can, and I'd pay the loan down only if there was money left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Wired and anxious. It's like standing on a platform when the train's late and you don't know if it's coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in the first month after hearing it was two years away?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my housemates to stop spending on takeaways and save, and I'd show them how to use the tools. Two of them would laugh and one would listen. I'd keep telling them anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the people you live with?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own timing. I'm only halfway through the first year, and every month I'm learning something the AI already does. A degree that takes three years starts to feel long when the world takes two.

say: I'd say it's the **biggest** thing that will ever happen, and governments need to act now.
I'd talk about it in every **conversation**.
think: Privately, it's the first one that really **scares** me: no data jobs for a first-timer by graduation.
Using AI daily means I'm not starting from **zero**.
do: Build a small **AI** tool that earns money, such as one for local cafes.
Increase **delivery** hours and save everything I can.
feel: **Wired** and anxious, like waiting for a late train.
S2.quote: A degree that takes three years starts to feel long when the world takes two.
fieldNote: He turns the shock into a **side income** plan and keeps studying.
His main fear is **timing**: three years of degree against a two-year deadline.

steps.text: Build a small AI tool to sell to local cafes
Increase delivery hours and save every spare pound
Stay in the degree while learning new AI skills
Show housemates how to use the tools

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's fast but manageable, and I'd keep pushing people to learn the tools. I'd say governments should start now, and universities should add AI to every course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd feel better than in the fast one, because I'd finish before the robots arrive. I'd still be in a market with fewer entry-level jobs, but I'd go in with strong AI skills and a good degree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree with a computing minor and build a portfolio of real projects. I'd save money from deliveries, apply for a masters, and look for placements in medical physics. I'd also try freelancing for small businesses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty energised. It's a race, but I think I'm ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years is enough for a degree. What would you do differently from the fast case?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the entry-level market collapses before I graduate. If the hospital physics jobs freeze and the data jobs go, I'd be stuck. So I'd keep a second option, maybe contract work or consulting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would worry you most in the five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd worry about my mum. My mum works in a payroll office, which is the kind of work AI would take early. Five years gives her time to retrain, and I'd help her pick a course.

say: I'd say it's fast but **manageable**, and universities should add AI to every course.
I'd keep pushing people to **learn** the tools.
think: Privately, I'd feel **better** than in the fast one, since I'd finish before robots arrive.
I'd go in with strong AI skills and a good **degree**.
do: Finish with a computing **minor** and build a portfolio of real projects.
Apply for a **masters** and try freelancing for small businesses.
feel: Pretty **energised**; a race where I think I'm ahead.
S3.quote: My mum works in a payroll office, which is the kind of work AI would take early.
fieldNote: He feels **ahead** of peers thanks to daily AI use and keeps a second option as insurance.
His main worry is his **mum's** payroll job.

steps.text: Finish the degree with a computing minor
Take freelance data jobs for small businesses
Help mum pick a retraining course
Apply for a masters in medical physics

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a huge gift. I'd say we should be rebuilding education around what AI can't do, like judgement, care and creativity. I'd want to be part of that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd feel good. I'd finish the degree, do a masters, probably work in medical physics for a few years or start my own small company. A decade lets me try three versions of my career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd study, take the best placements and build a company that uses AI for hospital scheduling. I'd save for a deposit, and help my mum retrain. And I'd keep learning, because the tools change every six months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and a bit excited. Ten years feels like a runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, what would you want to be doing by 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That people won't use the time. Everyone says they'll deal with it and then they don't. I'd worry about friends who stay stuck, and about people who can't afford to experiment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would still worry you even with that much time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The gap between students who can afford to take risks and those who can't. I'm lucky to have a scholarship, but one bad month of deliveries and I'm in trouble. Ten years is only an advantage if you can eat meanwhile.

say: I'd say a decade is a **gift**, and we should rebuild education around what AI can't do.
I'd want to be part of that **work**.
think: Privately, I'd feel **good**: a degree, a masters and then medical physics or my own company.
A decade lets me try three **versions** of my career.
do: Study, take the best **placements** and build a company that uses AI for hospital scheduling.
Save for a **deposit** and help my mum retrain.
feel: **Calm** and a bit excited; ten years feels like a runway.
S4.quote: Ten years is only an advantage if you can eat meanwhile.
fieldNote: The long **runway** suits his adaptive style: he plans a company and a deposit.
He recognises that thin money limits **risk-taking** even for people like him.

steps.text: Finish the degree and a masters in medical physics
Build a hospital scheduling tool with AI

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened? And is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one worries me most. Three years of degree against a two-year clock, and a mum whose payroll job could go first. What would help is a real income floor while people retrain, and universities that teach the tools instead of banning them. One thing you didn't ask: I'm optimistic mostly because I use the tools. I worry about the people who don't, and about me if I ever stop.

headlineQuote: I'm optimistic mostly because I use the tools. I worry about the people who don't, and about me if I ever stop.
portrait: Liam is a **physics** student on a medical physics track who delivers food by bike four evenings a week.
He uses AI every day, builds small **projects** and is comfortable changing course.
Centre in outlook, he wants **evidence** before a big switch but moves quickly once he has it.
His fear is **timing** and his mum's payroll job, and the thin money that limits how much risk he can take.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** AGI case worries him most: a three-year degree against a two-year clock, and mum's payroll job.
whatWouldHelp: A real **income** floor while people retrain, and universities that teach the tools.
